title: Paris, 1900–1913
subtitle: Quiet pianos, painted water and dancers who shake the floor

hero.caption: Claude Monet, Impression, soleil levant, 1872, Musée Marmottan Monet. An orange sun hangs over the boats in Le Havre’s misted harbour.

intro: Satie leaves a melody hanging over two quiet piano chords; twenty-five years later, Stravinsky makes an orchestra stamp. Between them lie Debussy’s sea and clouds, Ravel’s birds and plucked strings, and the dancers who brought the Ballets Russes to Paris.

stations.title: Satie leaves a note hanging
stations.text: Satie played the piano at the Chat Noir cabaret, then at the Auberge du Clou, where he met Debussy. His first Gymnopédie, written in 1888, takes its time: a bass note on the first beat, a soft chord on the second. G and D alternate below. Four bars pass before the melody arrives, and its long F♯ hangs over the changing chords. Later, a low E stays put while the harmony darkens beneath it. The first ending recovers a gentle brightness, closing on D major before the music starts again.

cues.text: The melody enters after four bars; its held F♯ floats above the alternating G and D bass notes.
The melody settles on E while three different chords pass beneath it.
The closing phrase falls from G to F♯; two full chords bring the first half to rest in D major.

stations.title: Gongs in Paris, bells at the piano
stations.text: At the 1889 Paris Exposition, Debussy heard Javanese gamelan: gongs ringing beneath quicker instrumental patterns. In the Revue musicale S.I.M. in 1913, he wrote that its counterpoint made Palestrina’s seem like “child’s play”. His Pagodes of 1903 had already brought gong-like bass notes to the piano. Here Marcelle Meyer plays La cathédrale engloutie, published in 1910. Bare fifths rise slowly, leaving long spaces for the notes to ring. As the left hand begins rolling beneath the ascending chords, the cathedral of Breton legend starts to emerge from the sea.

cues.text: Marcelle Meyer plays La cathédrale engloutie: bare piano fifths rise like bells sounding across water.
The left hand begins rolling in triplets beneath the rising chords; the cathedral emerges from the mist.

stations.title: Flute, harp and an orange sun

art.caption: Claude Monet, Impression, soleil levant, 1872. An orange sun and dark boats stand out against the mist over Le Havre’s harbour.

stations.text: Paris first heard Nuages in December 1900. Here, in the middle of the piece, flute and harp share a five-note melody over softly held strings, as if a patch of sky has cleared. The cor anglais then returns with its old, narrow phrase, and the sound draws in around it. Monet painted Impression, soleil levant from a hotel window in Le Havre in 1872. Dark boats sit close to the eye; the orange sun and its reflection stand out against the mist. Farther back, cranes and masts almost disappear into the morning haze.

cues.text: Flute and harp share a melody made from five notes, floating above softly held strings.
The cor anglais returns to its old phrase as the flute-and-harp tune fades.
The returning phrases grow shorter, with more air around each wind voice.

stations.title: Ravel’s strings snap, then sing
stations.text: Ravel finished his String Quartet in April 1903 and dedicated it to his teacher, Fauré. The scherzo begins with fingers on strings. Two violins, viola and cello pluck their notes, each with a little sting. A bowed melody then stretches over the continuing pizzicato, the long phrase riding above the short ones. Debussy was interested in how these four voices sat together. Writing to Ravel before the March 1904 première, he suggested a small adjustment to the playing: the viola could be a little quieter.

cues.text: Two violins, viola and cello pluck the dance into life, each short note sharply outlined.
The bowed melody stretches across the quick plucked notes, carrying a long breath above their sharp little steps.

stations.title: Hokusai’s wave on Debussy’s cover

art.file: File:Katsushika Hokusai - Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji- The Great Wave Off the Coast of Kanagawa - Google Art Project.jpg
art.caption: Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa, c. 1830–32, colour woodblock print. The wave arches over small boats, with Mount Fuji beyond.

stations.text: The United States Air Force Band plays the opening of La Mer in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription. A low B lies beneath the dawn; small phrases appear above it, separated by stretches of stillness. As the music begins to flow, groups of two and three notes cross one another. When Durand published the score in 1905, its cover carried an adapted detail of Hokusai’s wave. In the complete print, narrow boats lie under the curling crest. Far behind them, Mount Fuji stands beyond the reach of the water.

cues.text: Odom’s concert-band transcription opens over a low B, with small phrases stirring above it.
The low notes hold their ground while shorter phrases begin to move overhead.
The slow dawn opens into flowing motion; short calls gather over a running accompaniment.
Groups of two notes cross groups of three, giving the quiet movement a tug beneath its surface.

stations.title: Birds in the summer heat
stations.text: Ravel described the birds of Oiseaux tristes as lost in a dark forest during the hottest hours of summer. The piano begins high and alone, with a repeated B♭ and a tiny flourish. Beneath the next calls, the left hand moves in threes while the right hand divides its beat in two. A louder cry meets a distant, quiet answer. Ravel dedicated the piece to Ricardo Viñes, who first played Miroirs at the Salle Érard on 6 January 1906. When the opening call returns in D minor, held chords lie beneath it like shade.

cues.text: A high B♭ repeats softly, then opens into a small flourish; the left hand waits.
The left hand moves in threes beneath the right hand’s twos, circling under the bird’s call.
A loud call meets a distant, quiet answer while the lower notes keep turning.
The opening call returns in D minor, sheltered by softly held chords.

stations.title: Karsavina’s bird takes command

art.caption: Léon Bakst, costume design for the Ballets Russes production of The Firebird, 1910.

stations.text: On 25 June 1910, Tamara Karsavina danced The Firebird at the Paris Opéra, with choreography by Michel Fokine for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. In the Infernal Dance, the bird forces Kashchei and his creatures into motion. The United States Marine Band plays Thomas Knox’s concert-band arrangement here. Short figures jab across the pulse; displaced accents make the dance lurch, and the music keeps springing back. Bakst’s costume design puts the bird on paper, ready for a dancer to inhabit. A longer melody then stretches across the beat, while Kashchei remains caught in her spell.

cues.text: The Marine Band plays Thomas Knox’s arrangement of Kashchei’s forced dance: short phrases strike and spring back.
Sharp accents pull across the steady pulse, making the dance lurch.
A longer melody stretches across the beat after the clipped opening phrases.

stations.title: A bassoon above the orchestra
stations.text: On 29 May 1913, Pierre Monteux conducted the première of The Rite of Spring at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées. Nijinsky had choreographed the ballet for Diaghilev’s company. The music begins with a bassoon high in its range, winding through a melody drawn from a Lithuanian folk-song collection. Other winds crowd around it, each finding a separate path through the thicket. This recording brings Stravinsky himself to the podium, conducting the Columbia Symphony Orchestra in January 1960. Near the introduction’s end, the wind calls thin out and the opening bassoon tune comes back, briefly exposed before the stamping begins.

cues.text: A bassoon sings high in its range; other winds gradually gather around its winding tune.
Separate wind phrases overlap, cross and interrupt one another, crowding the opening melody.
The wind calls begin to thin out, leaving space around the bassoon before the dance.

stations.title: The strings stamp, the horns strike
stations.text: The strings stamp out the same chord at the opening of Augurs of Spring, pressing F♭ major against an E♭ dominant seventh. Horns strike selected attacks harder. The opening bars keep their steady 2/4 while the accents shift, leaving quiet strokes between the blows. In a letter to Nicholas Roerich on 26 September 1911, Stravinsky described an old woman in squirrel fur running in front of the dancers, stopping and interrupting their rhythm. He was composing this very dance with her before his eyes. Around the repeated tread, shorter phrases dart across the orchestra, and the horns strike again.

cues.text: The strings repeat their crowded chord; horns pick out certain strokes with extra force.
The dance opens in 2/4, with quiet strokes filling the uneven gaps between the accents.
The dance swells around its recurring figures, then draws back again.
A repeated tread holds beneath the shorter phrases, with the orchestra stamping and speaking at once.
